questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison that confuses a narrator with a period
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a comparison of a narrator with a period actually compares.
questions.stem: A comparison sets a Victorian diarist beside a medieval chronicler and asks what it actually compares.

options.text: the two texts' positions in their own centuries, since period is the truest common ground
options.misconception: treats shared period as the substance of a comparison

options.text: the two writers' habits of mind, since personality explains every difference in a record
options.misconception: reduces a comparison to the temperaments of two writers

options.text: the two ways of telling, since a narrator's voice belongs to a person, not to a century
the two sets of readers, since how a record was received settles what it means
options.misconception: confuses a text's reception with its narrative voice

questions.explanation: A narrator's way of telling belongs to a voice, not to a calendar, so the comparison should examine reporting habits. Period and reception are useful context but neither supplies the voice a reader actually hears.
questions.hint: Listen to the telling, not the date.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what one shared image means in two different traditions.

stimulus.body: Entry for 9 April: the road that winds appears in the romance I am reading and in the sermon the keeper's wife brought home. In the romance the road is a test the hero must take. In the sermon the road is a life that bends but keeps going. Same image, two shelves of the same library.

questions.stem: One image, a winding road, appears in a romance and in a sermon, and the logbook asks about the pairing.

options.text: The road means the same in both, since a winding road always stands for a difficult journey
options.misconception: believes one image carries one fixed symbolic value

options.text: The romance keeps the older sense and the sermon the newer, since traditions replace meanings
options.misconception: assumes a later tradition simply replaces an earlier sense

options.text: Each tradition invests the road in its own concerns, so the image is worked differently in each
The sermons simply borrow from romances, since preaching draws its images from stories
options.misconception: reduces the relation to one tradition borrowing from another

questions.explanation: Each tradition invests the image in its own concerns, so a winding road can be a trial in one book and a life in another. A fixed meaning, a timeline of replacement, and a simple borrowing story all ignore what each text is doing.
questions.hint: Ask what each tradition wants from the road.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what happens when one shared image works in opposite directions.
questions.stem: The beekeeper's note explains what happens when a shared image works in opposite directions.

answer.exemplar: When one image works in opposite directions in two texts, the shared thing is the picture itself and not the attitude to it. A hive may be a model of ordered labour in one book and a warning about slavery in another. The image supplies material for judgment, and each tradition supplies the judgment, so the difference lies in what each text wants the picture to do rather than in what the picture is.

questions.explanation: A shared image supplies material for judgment, not a fixed verdict, so opposite uses are not contradictions. The difference lies in what each text wants the image to do, which is why the pairing must be read for use, not for content.
questions.hint: Ask what each text wants the image to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how one word carries two separate emblematic meanings.
questions.stem: The word 'hive' carries two separate emblematic meanings in two older texts, and the log records the clash.

options.text: One meaning is the older and therefore the correct one, since emblems keep their first sense
options.misconception: insists the earliest sense of an emblem word is the true one

options.text: The word is being used loosely, since a careful writer picks one term for one thing
options.misconception: assumes a careful writer would not use one term for two things

options.text: Both senses belong to one emblem, since emblem books gather every association of a word
options.misconception: assumes one emblem can gather every association at once

options.text: Each text is using the word inside its own emblematic system, so the sense is fixed locally

questions.explanation: Each text draws on its own emblematic system, so the sense of a shared word is fixed by local context rather than by age or by the writer's care. One true sense, careless usage, and a single all-inclusive emblem each misdescribe the situation.
questions.hint: Read the emblem book that text belongs to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Finding a counterpart by traits or by office
questions.learningObjective: Explain what kind of matching makes two figures true counterparts.
questions.stem: A reader seeks a counterpart for a reclusive alchemist and the log asks what kind of matching is fair.

options.text: That the pair works by shared traits, since character rather than position is what readers remember
options.misconception: reduces counterpart finding to character traits alone

options.text: That the pair works by shared office, since two figures holding the same role invite the closest reading
options.misconception: treats shared office as the only sound basis for pairing

options.text: That the pair works only if both figures share traits and office together, which is rare
options.misconception: demands that traits and office always coincide in a pair

options.text: That the pair works only if the reader says which kind of matching is being used and why

questions.explanation: A counterpart is found either by traits or by office, and the comparison must declare which it is using and why. Traits alone, office alone, and a rule that demands both each narrow or confuse what the pairing can show.
questions.hint: Declare which kind of match you make.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A theme claimed as universal
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a claim of a universal theme assumes.
questions.stem: A critic claims that every age longs for home, and the logbook asks what that claim assumes.

options.text: That a theme is a topic, so that any culture dwelling on home proves the longing is universal
options.misconception: equates a repeated topic with a universal human need

options.text: That a theme is a mood, so that any reader who feels homesick confirms the claim
options.misconception: treats one reader's feeling as evidence of universality

options.text: That a theme is a figure of speech, so that a poem's use of the word settles the question
options.misconception: believes a single repeated word proves a universal theme

options.text: That a theme is an argument, so that a claim of universality must be argued rather than asserted

questions.explanation: A theme is an argument the text makes, so a claim of universality is a claim that must be argued across cases. Treating theme as topic, mood, or repeated word lets a few examples pass for a proof about everyone.
questions.hint: A theme is an argument, not a topic.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme
questions.learningObjective: Identify what would complicate a claim of a universal theme.

stimulus.body: Entry for 2 July: the essay in the reading room says that the longing for home is the oldest story there is. I have been trying to find a text that does not want a home at all, or wants one it must not have, and there are two on the shelf that will not fit the claim. I want to write down what they do before I argue anything.

questions.stem: A reader challenges a universal claim about exile and the log asks what would complicate it.

options.text: A text in which home is refused, since a refusal shows the longing is not always present
options.misconception: treats one refusal as proof that no longing exists anywhere

options.text: A text in which home is feared, since the same idea works with the sign reversed
options.misconception: confuses a reversed feeling with a different theme entirely

options.text: A text from an unfamiliar period, since the more periods the more certain the theme
options.misconception: believes the number of periods settles a claim of universality

options.text: A text in which home is complicated, since a qualified case resists the claim it seems to support

questions.explanation: The cases that complicate a universal claim are qualified ones, where the theme appears but is refused, altered, or made uncertain. A single reversal proves only that the theme is not simple, and more periods add cases rather than certainty.
questions.hint: Look for the case that qualifies the claim.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison that confuses a narrator with a period
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a narrator must not be read as a period.
questions.stem: An entry from the spring records why a narrator should never be read as a period.

answer.exemplar: A narrator is a person telling, while a period is a stretch of history, and the two answer to different things. A narrator has habits of attention, a vocabulary and a set of worries; a period has institutions, print practices and shared assumptions. When a comparison slides from one to the other, the reader gets a general picture of an age instead of a reading of how one mind reports what it saw.

questions.explanation: A narrator has habits of attention and vocabulary, while a period has institutions and shared assumptions. Sliding one for the other replaces a reading of one mind's reporting with a general portrait of an age.
questions.hint: Tellings and eras are different kinds of thing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one image carries different force in two traditions.
questions.stem: A candle flame stands for grief in one poem and for vigilance in another, and the entry asks why.

options.text: Because the two poems were written in different centuries, so images change their meanings over time
options.misconception: attributes every change of image to the passage of time

options.text: Because each tradition asks a different question of the flame, so the same picture serves each purpose
Because one poet is subtler than the other, and only a weak poet needs a stock image
options.misconception: judges the difference in image use by the poet's quality

options.text: Because candles were cheaper in one century, so the flame was more readily available to writers
options.misconception: explains an image's force by the cost of its object

questions.explanation: The force of an image comes from the question each text asks of it, so a flame can register a loss in one poem and a watchful presence in another. Centuries, poetic quality, and the price of wax describe circumstances rather than the image's work.
questions.hint: Ask what question each text puts to the flame.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what makes two opposite uses of one image intelligible.
questions.stem: A threshold crossing means departure in one story and arrival in another, and the log asks what the difference rests on.

options.text: On the direction of travel, since a threshold is a line and a line has a way
options.misconception: reduces the difference to the geometry of the threshold

options.text: On who is doing the crossing, since the same doorway serves a departing person and an arriving one
options.misconception: blames the direction of travel for the whole difference

options.text: On the period of each story, since earlier stories say goodbye and later ones say hello
options.misconception: explains the difference by the era of each story

options.text: On what each story wants the crossing to accomplish, since the image answers the plot's need

questions.explanation: A shared image answers the need of the text that uses it, so a threshold becomes departure or arrival according to what the plot requires. Direction, the person crossing, and the period of composition are real details that do not settle the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what each plot needs from the doorway.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one term names two separate emblems.
questions.stem: A single term, 'wasp', names an emblem of malice in one manual and a warning sign in another.

options.text: That the two emblems belong to different systems, so the shared word needs its manual to be understood
That the word was mistranscribed in one manual, since no word can carry two emblematic senses
options.misconception: treats a double emblem as a copying error

options.text: That the earlier emblem was the true one and the later a debased version of it
options.misconception: assumes the earliest emblem is the authentic one

options.text: That both emblems are really one idea expressed twice, since malice and warning are near neighbours
options.misconception: merges two emblems because the words feel related

questions.explanation: One term can name two emblems when it belongs to two emblematic systems, so the shared word only makes sense with its manual in hand. A copying error, an original and its corruption, and a near-synonymy all collapse distinctions the systems keep apart.
questions.hint: A word needs its system to be read.

questions.topic: Finding a counterpart by traits or by office
questions.learningObjective: Identify when two figures sharing an office are not counterparts.
questions.stem: Two figures share a title of office but nothing else, and the log asks whether they are counterparts.

options.text: They are, since the office is what a reader meets first and the rest is decoration
options.misconception: treats a shared title as sufficient for a pairing

options.text: They are not, since a shared office without shared traits produces no useful comparison
They are, provided the two texts were written in the same century and so share a world
options.misconception: believes shared period completes a counterpart pair

options.text: They are not, since the office in one text carries duties the other office never had
options.misconception: rejects pairing only when the offices differ in scope

questions.explanation: A counterpart needs enough shared ground for a comparison to bite, and an office without shared traits gives none. Shared period does not supply it, and a difference in duties disqualifies the pair rather than settling the matter.
questions.hint: Shared ground must do some work.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A theme claimed as universal
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a sweeping claim about power assumes.

stimulus.body: Entry for 19 January: the essay on the table says that power has always corrupted the people who hold it. It sounds like a fact about people. Then I think of the two small books on the same shelf where the officer keeps his accounts honestly and nobody notices him at all, and the claim starts to feel like it is really a claim about visibility.

questions.stem: An essay asserts that power corrupts in every civilisation, and the beekeeper's log tests the claim.

options.text: The claim is simply false, since one honest officer in any book disproves a universal statement
options.misconception: treats a single counterexample as a complete refutation

options.text: The claim is true in most cases, since most examples support it and the rest are exceptions
options.misconception: counts examples instead of testing what the claim says

options.text: The claim confuses being noticed with being corrupted, since visibility is what a story rewards
The claim cannot be tested at all, since no reader can judge corruption in a stranger's world
options.misconception: denies that a claim about behaviour can be examined

questions.explanation: A universal claim about power can smuggle in a second claim about visibility, since stories show what is noticed. Counting examples or dismissing the whole claim leaves the real work undone, and a single counterexample does not settle a statement about every case.
questions.hint: Ask what a story can show about the unobserved.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme
questions.learningObjective: Explain what complicates a claim that a theme belongs to everyone.
questions.stem: A note of 22 March explains what complicates a claim that a theme belongs to all people.

answer.exemplar: A theme that is claimed for everybody is complicated by the texts in which it appears only partly, or with the parts the claimant has left out. The claim is a claim about a pattern across works, so it must be tested against the awkward cases: the works where the theme is absent, the ones where it is held at a distance, and the ones where the same words serve a different idea entirely. Those cases do not refute the theme; they mark its edges.

questions.explanation: A claim about a universal theme must survive the awkward cases, where the theme is absent, held at a distance, or serving another idea. Those cases mark its edges rather than refute it, which is why a sweeping claim needs testing rather than repetition.
questions.hint: Test the claim against the awkward cases.

questions.topic: A comparison that confuses a narrator with a period
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a comparison by date rather than by voice establishes.
questions.stem: A comparison places a sixteenth-century diarist next to a modern memoirist and asks what is being compared.

options.text: Two documents of private record, since the century of each has nothing to do with the comparison
options.misconception: dismisses period as irrelevant to any comparison at all

options.text: Two habits of private observation, since recording privately is a single continuous practice
options.misconception: treats private recording as one unbroken practice across centuries

options.text: Two modes of self-narration, since each writer shapes a self that the other never had to shape
Two kinds of reader, since the diary and the memoir were written for different kinds of attention
options.misconception: confuses a text's readership with its mode of self-narration

questions.explanation: A comparison of two diarists is properly a comparison of two modes of self-narration, each shaping a self for its own conditions. Century, continuity of private practice, and readership are context, and none of them replaces the comparison of voices.
questions.hint: Compare the selves each writer constructs.

questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what pairing one image across traditions reveals about each.
questions.stem: One bird appears in a fable and a psalm, and the log asks what the pairing reveals about traditions.

options.text: That the two traditions share an inheritance of images, since fables and psalms draw on common stock
options.misconception: assumes the traditions simply share a common stock of images

options.text: That the psalm borrows the fable, since a later writer improved the older figure
options.misconception: decides a direction of borrowing without any evidence

options.text: That the bird is a shared property, so the meaning attached to it must be common too
options.misconception: confuses a shared object with a shared meaning

options.text: That each tradition uses the bird for its own work, so the pairing shows two systems rather than one

questions.explanation: Pairing one image across traditions shows two systems at work, since each uses the bird for its own ends. A common inheritance, a direction of borrowing, and a shared meaning attached to a shared object each assume more than the pair can support.
questions.hint: Two systems, not one shared stock.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one image carries opposed charges in two traditions.
questions.stem: An entry records how the same image carries opposed charges in two neighbouring traditions.

answer.exemplar: Opposed charges in one image are not a contradiction but a division of labour. The picture of the hive can stand for the industry the village praises and for the coercion a later writer wants readers to notice, and both uses draw on the same visible facts. What separates them is the judgment each text is making, and a reader who treats the image as a single verdict will lose the argument that the pair can produce.

questions.explanation: Opposed charges in one image are a division of labour, since both uses draw on the same visible facts while making different judgments. Treating the image as one fixed verdict loses the argument the pair can produce.
questions.hint: Look for the judgment in each use.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate how to read one term that serves two emblem books.
questions.stem: Two emblem books use the same term for a lantern and for a spy, and the log asks how to read it.

options.text: Read the term loosely, since emblem books reuse vocabulary and no tight sense can be meant
options.misconception: assumes emblem books have no fixed meanings to read

options.text: Read the later book as correcting the earlier, since books of emblems improved in quality
options.misconception: ranks emblem books by presumed improvement over time

options.text: Read whichever sense suits the writer's argument, since the image is chosen for effect
options.misconception: lets an argument choose the sense after the fact

options.text: Read each sense within its own book, since an emblem is fixed by the system that supplies it

questions.explanation: An emblem is fixed by the system supplying it, so each sense must be read inside its own book. Loose reading, ranking the books, and choosing a sense to suit an argument all abandon the system that makes the emblem legible.
questions.hint: Each book supplies its own sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Finding a counterpart by traits or by office
questions.learningObjective: Apply the distinction between trait-based and office-based matching.

stimulus.body: Entry for 14 March: I want a counterpart for the archivist in the second book. She spends her life cataloguing other people's papers and says she has never kept any of her own. The obvious candidate is the clerk in the older story, who burns his own ledger at the end. Same job, same relation to records, and I think that is exactly why the pairing might work.

questions.stem: A reader wants a counterpart for a quiet archivist and the logbook asks what counts as a match.

options.text: The clerk, since both hold the same office and spend their lives among other people's papers
options.misconception: treats a shared office as the whole of the match

options.text: The clerk, since both feel the pull of order and of record-keeping for its own sake
options.misconception: matches on temperament and ignores the office

options.text: The clerk, provided the comparison is declared to be about office and not about character
Neither, since a counterpart must share traits and office together, which no pair ever does
options.misconception: demands that traits and office always coincide

questions.explanation: The archivist and the clerk make a useful pair on the basis of office, and the reader must say so rather than let the pairing drift into a claim about character. Traits alone, office alone, and a rule requiring both each weaken what the comparison can show.
questions.hint: Say which kind of match you are making.

questions.topic: A theme claimed as universal
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a claim about all great books leaves out.
questions.stem: An essay says that all great books are about love, and the log asks what the claim leaves out.

options.text: That the claim names the theme in advance, so the critic never has to face a book that resists it
options.misconception: treats a naming of the theme as a substitute for reading

options.text: That the claim is really about love's varieties, since a wide word covers a wide range of books
options.misconception: expands a term until it can no longer be tested

options.text: That the claim needs no evidence, since the greatness of the books is already agreed
options.misconception: takes the critic's premises for granted

options.text: That the claim omits books whose interest is in power, work, law, or knowledge rather than love

questions.explanation: A sweeping claim about love leaves out the many books whose interest lies in power, work, law, or knowledge, and those exclusions are what should be tested. Naming the theme in advance, widening the word until it covers everything, and borrowing the critic's premises all avoid the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask which books the claim leaves out.

questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme
questions.learningObjective: Identify what exceptions establish about a universal claim.
questions.stem: A universal claim about war meets three exceptions, and the log asks what those exceptions establish.

options.text: That the claim is false, since three exceptions outweigh any number of supporting cases
options.misconception: lets three exceptions overrule a wider pattern of cases

options.text: That the theme is present everywhere but valued differently in different places and periods
That the exceptions are errors, since a text that does not fit the claim must be misread
options.misconception: dismisses awkward cases as misreadings

options.text: That the theme does not exist, since a claim that needs exceptions has no theme at all
options.misconception: treats qualified evidence as the absence of a theme

questions.explanation: Exceptions to a universal claim usually show that the theme is present but weighted differently across cases. They do not overturn a wider pattern, nor do they prove the theme absent, and calling them misreadings avoids the question rather than answering it.
questions.hint: Exceptions show weighting, not absence.

options.text: Because both accounts describe the same year, the date is the only shared fact a reader can use
options.misconception: believes a shared event substitutes for a shared voice

options.text: Because the two writers belong to one age, so their accounts form a single historical record
options.misconception: collapses two writers into one historical record

options.misconception: offers shared vocabulary as the only workable test

options.text: Because the accounts are separated by generations, so the comparison must be made between voices

questions.explanation: When two accounts are separated by generations, a date-based pairing compares an era with a voice and tells the reader little. A shared event, a shared age, and shared vocabulary are each partial facts that do not settle what the accounts do together.
questions.hint: Compare the two tellings, not the years.

questions.stem: A plough appears in a plough-song and a political allegory, and the log asks what the two do with it.

options.misconception: insists working objects never carry figurative work

questions.hint: Ask what each text asks of the plough.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an emblem can warn and welcome at once.
questions.stem: The logbook explains how the same emblem can warn and welcome at once.

answer.exemplar: One emblem can warn and welcome at once because it holds two readings that a single text chooses between by the company it keeps. A hive stands for order and for swarming; a gate stands for shelter and for siege. The point is not that the emblem is contradictory, since it is a picture with several possible uses, but that a text selects among those uses by the situation it builds around the image, and the selection is what a reader must describe.

questions.explanation: An emblem holds several possible uses, and a text selects among them by the situation it builds around the image. That selection, not a contradiction inside the picture, is what a reader must describe when an emblem seems to work in two directions at once.
questions.hint: Watch which reading the context selects.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how context separates two senses of a shared term.

stimulus.body: Entry for 8 November: the same almanac word appears over the picture of a bee and over a picture of a man hiding behind a hedge. I assumed a copying error and checked the pages twice. The printer says the word is a general term for something that stings or stings in the way, and the two illustrations use it differently on purpose.

questions.stem: Two almanacs use one word for a bee and for a deceit, and the entry asks what separates them.

options.text: The subject of the picture, since an illustration settles which sense its word carries
options.misconception: believes the illustration alone determines the sense of the term

options.text: Nothing separates them, since one term cannot properly carry two emblematic senses
options.misconception: insists a term can hold only one emblematic sense

questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a theme that recurs everywhere from one confined to a tradition.
questions.stem: A note distinguishes a theme that recurs everywhere from a theme that recurs in one tradition only.

answer.exemplar: A theme that recurs in one tradition only is localised, and it is localised in a way that can be described: it depends on that tradition's inherited material, its habits of address, and the expectations its readers brought to it. A theme that recurs across unrelated traditions is a different kind of thing, because its recurrence is not explained by common inheritance. The test is therefore not how often a theme appears, but whether the appearance is explained by something the traditions share.

questions.explanation: The test is not how often a theme appears but whether its recurrence is explained by what the traditions share. Localised themes depend on inherited material and reader expectations, while a theme recurring across unrelated traditions needs a different explanation.

stimulus.body: Entry for 27 December: I wanted to set a court chronicler beside a diarist of the next century because both write about the same winter of trouble. On the page it looked convincing. The pairing had been made by the calendar, not by anything in the writing.

options.misconception: assumes one event produces one response in every witness

options.text: That the chronicler's courtly attention and the diarist's domestic attention are two views of one mind
options.misconception: merges two distinct attentions into a single consciousness

options.text: That matching the century is enough, since two records of the same winter are the same record
options.misconception: believes a shared event makes two records interchangeable

options.text: That a shared event invites a comparison of habits of mind, which the calendar cannot supply

questions.explanation: A shared event invites a comparison of habits of mind, and the calendar cannot supply those habits; the pairing here was made by date alone. One event with one response, a merged consciousness, and interchangeable records each miss what the two writers actually do.

questions.topic: Finding a counterpart by traits or by office
questions.learningObjective: Explain how traits and office differ as grounds for pairing.
questions.stem: An entry explains how traits and office differ as grounds for calling two figures counterparts.

answer.exemplar: Traits and office answer different questions about a figure. Office asks what the world requires of the person and what the person may therefore do, while traits ask how the person tends to act, which can run against the office entirely. A comparison built on office is about pressures and permissions, and a comparison built on traits is about disposition and habit. The two can cross, since a gentle person may hold a hard office, and the reader should say which basis is in play before drawing conclusions.

questions.explanation: Office asks what the world requires of a figure and traits ask how the figure tends to act, and the two can cross. Declaring which basis is in play keeps a comparison about pressures from turning into a claim about character.
questions.hint: Say which basis your comparison uses.

stimulus.body: Entry for 5 October: the pamphlet on the desk says every longing is for a lost childhood. It is a beautiful sentence and I have read it three times. options.text: The claim is refuted, since two counterexamples are enough to destroy a universal statement
options.misconception: believes two counterexamples destroy a universal claim

options.text: The claim survives, since the examples are unusual and universal claims concern the common case
options.misconception: rescues a universal claim by calling its counterexamples rare

options.text: The claim narrows to the longing for an earlier time, and the other two cases ask for something else
The claim cannot be examined, since longing is private and no reader can check another person's
options.misconception: treats longing as private and therefore untestable

questions.explanation: The counterexamples show the claim must be narrowed, since a longing for an unseen harbour is not a longing for a lost childhood. Destroying a universal claim needs more than two cases, rarity does not rescue it, and privacy does not make it untestable.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how one image serves an accusation in one place and a welcome in another.
questions.stem: The beekeeper notes how one image serves an accusation in one village and a welcome in the next.

answer.exemplar: The same image can be an accusation in one village and a welcome in the next because the swarm is a fact of the world that each community reads from its own side of the argument. Where hives are kept as a livelihood, the image of an ordered colony is welcome; where hives stand for the loss of common rights, the same ordered colony is a sign of what has been taken. questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme

questions.stem: An entry describes what a competing tradition adds to a theme claimed for everybody.

answer.exemplar: A competing tradition adds pressure to a theme claimed for everybody, because it puts the theme where it does not fit easily. If the claim is that people fear the unknown, a tradition that treats the unknown as a necessary teacher shows the theme in a shape the claim never described, and the fear is still present but no longer the whole of what the situation contains. The added pressure is what turns a claim about a theme into a claim about one tradition's handling of it.

questions.explanation: A competing tradition adds pressure by putting the theme where it does not fit easily, so the theme appears in a shape the claim never described. The added pressure distinguishes a claim about the theme from a claim about one tradition's handling of it.

answer.exemplar: A theme's universality is best argued from what it leaves out, because a claim that everything supports a theme and nothing sits awkwardly with it has told the reader nothing. questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reader can tell a narrator's period from a narrator's voice.
questions.stem: The logbook sets out how a reader can tell a narrator's period from a narrator's voice.

answer.exemplar: A narrator's period shows in what the narrator takes for granted: the offices that exist, the roads that do, the books a person would have had, and the dangers a person would have mentioned without a second thought. A narrator's voice shows in the habits of attention: what is noticed, what is passed over, the order in which things are remembered, the words the writer reaches for and the ones they refuse. The first set can be dated from outside; the second can only be heard from inside the text.

questions.explanation: A narrator's period shows in what the narrator takes for granted, which can be dated from outside, while a voice shows in habits of attention, which can only be heard inside the text. Conflating them replaces a reading of the teller with a description of an age.
questions.hint: Ask what the narrator takes for granted.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two traditions make of one shared image.

stimulus.body: Entry for 21 March: the swarm turns up in the sermon the family copied out and in the satire printed in the yard behind the inn. The sermon takes the swarm for the good of the hive, saying that no bee is idle and none is solitary. The satire takes it for the ruin of the orchard, saying that where they gather the branches are stripped. One swarm, two verdicts, and the bees themselves have not changed.

questions.stem: An image of a swarm appears in a sermon and a satire, and the entry asks what each makes of it.

options.text: The sermon praises shared labour, since the hive models an order worth imitating
The satire praises shared labour too, since satire usually hides a compliment in its complaint
options.misconception: insists satire must contain a disguised compliment

options.text: The sermon is the older text, so the satire merely copies its image for effect
options.misconception: assumes age explains the second use of an image

options.text: Neither image is about bees, since writers use pictures only when they mean the creatures themselves
options.misconception: insists images can only be read literally

questions.explanation: The sermon reads the swarm as shared labour worth imitating, while the satire reads the same swarm as the ruin of the orchard, and the difference lies in what each text is arguing for. Disguised compliments, age, and literal-mindedness each miss that disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask what each text argues for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Identify what governs two opposed charges for one image.
questions.stem: A shared image of frost melts in one version and hardens in another, and the log asks what governs that.

options.text: The season in which each story is set, since frost acts differently in winter and spring
options.misconception: blames the season for the image's work in the text

options.text: The author of each version, since one writer is gentler than the other
options.misconception: explains the difference by the author's temperament

options.text: The publisher's series, since a series fixes how an image should be read
options.misconception: believes a publisher's series determines an image's meaning

options.text: The situation each version builds, since the image serves whatever the plot requires

questions.explanation: The image serves whatever the situation each version builds, so frost can soften a loss in one story and harden a resolve in another. Season, authorial temperament, and publishing series are external facts that do not govern the image's work.
questions.hint: Ask what each version needs from the frost.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one word carries two emblematic traditions.
questions.stem: One word carries an emblem of war in one text and an emblem of trade in another, and the log compares them.

options.text: That the word sits in two emblematic systems, so its sense is settled by the book it appears in
That war and trade are close enough in meaning for one emblem to cover both senses
options.misconception: merges two emblems because the concerns seem adjacent

options.text: That the war emblem is the original and the trade one a later softening of it
options.misconception: presumes a degeneration from a warlike original meaning

options.text: That the word is a common one, so its sense cannot be pinned down in either text
options.misconception: believes a common word cannot be given a definite sense

questions.explanation: The word sits inside two emblematic systems, and each book settles which sense is in play. Adjacency of meaning, a presumed original and its softening, and the commonplace nature of the word all resist what the local apparatus can show.
questions.hint: Let each book fix its own sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Finding a counterpart by traits or by office
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes two figures true rather than convenient counterparts.
questions.stem: An entry sets out what makes two figures true counterparts rather than convenient ones.

answer.exemplar: A true counterpart is not chosen because the pairing flatters the argument but because the two figures occupy a comparable position under comparable pressure, so that what one does can be tested against what the other does. The trouble with convenient counterparts is that they agree too easily: the traits selected are the flattering ones, the office chosen is the one that makes the difference look like a virtue, and the comparison ends in confirmation rather than in anything a reader could have got wrong. A good pairing can embarrass the thesis that produced it.

questions.explanation: A true counterpart occupies a comparable position under comparable pressure, so what one does can be tested against what the other does. Convenient counterparts agree too easily, and a good pairing is one that can embarrass the argument that proposed it.
questions.hint: Try to embarrass the pairing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A theme claimed as universal
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a corpus-wide claim about endings.
questions.stem: A claim that every ending in the corpus is a return home is examined in the log.

options.text: It is safe, since the corpus was chosen by a reader who knows what endings contain
options.misconception: trusts a self-selected corpus as a fair sample

options.text: It is safe, since a return home is the ending audiences have always wanted most
options.misconception: grounds a corpus claim in what audiences prefer

options.text: It is doubtful, since the corpus on the shelf is the part of the writing this reader owns
It must be wrong, since no author in history could have written the same ending twice
options.misconception: insists that repetition of an ending is always impossible

questions.explanation: The claim is doubtful because the corpus is whatever the reader owns, so the evidence was never gathered in a way that could test a claim about all endings. Trust in the sample, audience preference, and an impossibility about repetition each substitute a stance for a test.
questions.hint: Ask how the corpus was gathered.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What complicates a claim of a universal theme
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a dissenting text does to a universal claim.
questions.stem: The log asks what a dissenting text does to a theme claimed for all readers.

options.text: It proves the theme false, since one dissenting voice outweighs the many who agree
options.misconception: lets one dissenting text outweigh a wider agreement

options.text: It has no effect, since a theme's universality was already settled by the readers who agreed
options.misconception: treats a settled consensus as immune to a dissenting text

options.text: It shows the theme was never universal, since all themes are the property of one group
options.misconception: replaces a universal claim with a claim that no theme is shared

options.text: It forces the theme to be stated more exactly, since the claim must now cover the dissenter too

questions.explanation: A dissenting text forces the theme to be stated more exactly, because a claim for all readers must now cover the dissenter as well. Outweighing a wider agreement, immunity by consensus, and the replacement of the claim by a narrower one each dodge that work.
questions.hint: Make the claim cover the dissenter.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison that confuses a narrator with a period
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two letters of different kinds are not one document.
questions.stem: A reader treats a Renaissance letter and a modern letter as one kind of document, and the log objects.

options.text: Because letters differ in length across the centuries, so the shorter ones are less substantial
options.misconception: judges a letter's worth by its length

options.text: Because each letter answers a different set of expectations about who is reading it
Because the earlier letter was written by hand and the later one by machine, which changes everything
options.misconception: believes the writing instrument settles a text's reading

options.text: Because only one of them was ever intended to be read by anybody other than its writer
options.misconception: insists letters are always private by nature

questions.explanation: Each letter answers a different set of expectations about its reader, and that difference in address is what the comparison must notice. Length, writing instrument, and privacy each rest on a general truth that does not bear on how the letters work.
questions.hint: Ask who each letter was written for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two traditions invest in one shared image.
questions.stem: A mirror appears in a romance and a sermon, and the log asks what each tradition invests in it.

options.text: The romance holds it as vanity, since looking at oneself is treated as pride there
The romance treats the mirror as a plot device, since reflections are needed for the disguise
options.misconception: treats an image as a mere device of the plot

options.text: Both treat it as vanity, since every age has been suspicious of self-regard
options.misconception: assumes one attitude toward self-regard in every age

options.text: Neither is symbolic, since mirrors in stories are only things a character happens to look into
options.misconception: insists a repeated object stays purely literal

questions.explanation: The romance holds the mirror as vanity while the sermon invests it as a figure for self-knowledge, since each tradition builds its own concerns into the object. A plot device, one age's suspicion, and literal-mindedness each refuse the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what each tradition wants from a mirror.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a shared image can hold opposite charges without contradiction.
questions.stem: The logbook explains why a shared image can carry opposite charges without contradiction.

answer.exemplar: Opposite charges in one image are not a contradiction because an image is not a statement but a piece of material that a text argues with. The picture of a swarm, a threshold, a hive, or a plough holds a set of possible associations, and a text draws on some of them and declines others, so a reader who arrives expecting one fixed verdict will find the image contradictory when it is merely being used. The opposition lies between two texts and their arguments, not inside the picture.

questions.explanation: An image is material that a text argues with rather than a statement, so opposing charges belong to two texts and their arguments, not to the picture. Arriving with a fixed verdict is what makes an image seem contradictory when it is only being used.
questions.hint: The opposition is between texts, not pictures.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate which reading of a shared term its context supports.
questions.stem: Two emblem manuals gloss one word differently, and the entry asks which reading the context supports.

options.text: The reading whose motto and verse belong to the same manual, since the local text decides
The reading in the older manual, since age preserves what later books garbled
options.misconception: trusts age to settle the sense of an emblem word

options.text: The reading with the better known motto, since famous verses are more likely to be right
options.misconception: judges a reading by the fame of its motto

options.text: Whichever the writer's intention favours, since the author decided the sense once and for all
options.misconception: assumes one fixed authorial decision governs a whole emblem tradition

questions.explanation: The manual's own motto and verse decide which reading is in play, since the local apparatus was made to support it. Age, the fame of a motto, and a single authorial decision each misplace the authority that settles the sense.
questions.hint: Keep the gloss with its own manual.
